**Executive summary**

Donald J. Trump is the incumbent President of the United States, having assumed office on January 20, 2025, and serving a term that extends through January 20, 2029 [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) ; multiple government, media and public records list him as the sitting president in 2026 [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.
org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States) and the White House website presents his administration as the current executive leadership [[3]](https://www.whitehouse.gov/) . Reporting and aggregated reference pages document both the administration's policy agenda and the legal and political controversies surrounding it, so any assessment of "who is president" must name the officeholder and acknowledge active disputes and ongoing litigation [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) .

Accurate Inaccurate

**1\. The holder of the office: a clear identification of the incumbent**

The person who currently occupies the U.S. presidency is Donald J. Trump, identified across official and reference sources as the President who took office January 20, 2025 [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.
org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States) , and who is listed as the 45th and 47th president in White House materials and public reference pages that track incumbency [[3]](https://www.whitehouse.gov/) [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States) . Multiple civic and government-oriented sites that compile contemporary political data also register Trump as the sitting president and note the 2025 inauguration date that begins his current term [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) [[5]](https://whowaspresident.com/2026) .

**2\. How he came to occupy the office: election and transition context**

Public summaries and election guides describe the electoral context that produced the 2025 inauguration, with reporting and archival resources cataloging the 2024–2025 campaign cycle and the formal transfer of power that occurred in January 2025 [[6]](https://researchguides.oakton.edu/c.php?
g=597133&p=4132838) [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) . Reference sites recount the continuity of democratic procedures that result in an inauguration following a certified election, and identify January 20 as the date the new presidential term legally begins, which is consistent with the recorded start date for this administration [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States) . Where sources discuss controversies connected to the prior administration and to legal challenges surrounding election-related actions, they do so while still recognizing the formal outcome that placed the current president in office [[1]](https://www.govtrack.us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) .

**3\. What the administration is doing and how sources describe it**
Contemporary reporting and institutional summaries outline an active and interventionist administration agenda, from trade and energy policy to foreign military actions, with the White House describing domestic accomplishments while media and encyclopedic sources document sweeping executive orders and aggressive foreign-policy moves [[3]](https://www.whitehouse.gov/) [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) . For example, encyclopedic reporting catalogs heavy use of executive action and numerous lawsuits challenging those actions, noting hundreds of legal cases filed that by mid-January 2026 had produced varied outcomes and many pending suits [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) . Official White House messaging characterizes the administration’s agenda as a period of economic growth and strategic initiative [[3]](https://www.whitehouse.
gov/) , while outside analysis highlights contentious decisions—tariffs, military strikes, and other measures—that have produced domestic and international pushback [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) [[8]](https://globalaffairs.org/commentary/analysis/trump-20-enters-2026-full-force) .

**4\. Contested elements and legal disputes that shape public understanding**

The record shows significant legal and political contestation surrounding the administration: courts have ruled on the legality of tariffs and other policies, and many executive actions have been litigated, with mixed results in courtrooms across the country [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) .
Reference reporting notes a major appeals-court decision limiting claimed powers used to justify tariffs and documents ongoing litigation challenging tens to hundreds of the administration’s measures [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) . These documented disputes do not negate who holds the office but shape how the presidency is exercised and perceived, and they explain why public records about policy often come paired with court rulings and legal analysis [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) .

**5\. The narrower answer and why caveats matter**

At the narrow factual level required by the question, the President of the United States is Donald J. Trump, inaugurated January 20, 2025, and recorded as the incumbent in governmental and reference sources through 2026 [[1]](https://www.govtrack.
us/congress/other-people/donald_trump/412733) [[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States) . The caveats worth noting are not about who occupies the office but about how that office is being used and disputed in courts and international relations—context that informs what "who is president" means in practice as much as it does on paper [[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) [[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump) .
